congeal

/kun-JEEL/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Congeal means to thicken or solidify, especially when a liquid cools into a solid mass.

The gravy forgotten on the counter began to congeal into a pale, rubbery layer.

Worked Example

A cook poured the hot drippings from a roasting pan into a metal bowl and set it near an open window. Within an hour the liquid had turned cloudy at the edges, then stiffened toward the center. By morning it had thickened into a solid pale cake that a spoon could stand upright in. Nothing had been added to it; the fat only needed to cool in order to congeal.

A liquid cooled and set into a solid mass with nothing added to it, which is exactly what congeal describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

solidify: Solidify means to become fully firm or solid, and it also covers deliberate processes and figurative ones - concrete solidifies, plans solidify, support solidifies. Congeal is narrower and more physical: a cooling liquid sets into a soft, often unappetizing mass. Concrete solidifies into something you can stand on; leftover gravy merely congeals.

coagulate: Coagulate describes a liquid clotting into clumps and curds through a chemical change - blood coagulates at a wound, milk coagulates when acid hits it. Congeal is about temperature: a liquid cools and sets smoothly into one soft mass. Blood coagulates whether warm or cold; gravy congeals simply because it cools.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

liquefy: to turn into a liquid

melt: to soften and become liquid, usually through heat

Where it sits · how completely the liquid sets — thicken → congeal → harden

thicken vs. congeal: To thicken is only to grow denser while still flowing, whereas to congeal is to set into a mass that no longer pours at all.

harden vs. congeal: Congealing leaves behind a soft, spoonable solid, but hardening goes further, leaving something firm and unyielding.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con

Prefix — con: together, thoroughly

Root — geal

Root — geal: from Latin gelare, to freeze (the root behind gel and gelatin)

Put it together

Put it together: Congeal comes from Latin congelare, from con- ('together, thoroughly') plus gelare ('to freeze'), the root behind gel and gelatin, so it literally means 'to freeze thoroughly.' Watch out for one thing in this unit: the -al ending on congeal is not the suffix -al ('characteristic of') at all. It is simply part of the Latin verb gelare, which makes congeal a useful false friend to keep in mind while you study the real -al words here.

Use the root in a new word: gelatin

Use the root in a new word: gelatin: Cooks rely on gelatin to make a broth set into a wobbling block, a word that carries the same Latin gelare, 'to freeze,' found inside congeal.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral register; common in cooking, biology, and figurative writing

In ordinary use congeal is intransitive: a liquid congeals on its own as it cools, rather than someone congealing it. Writers also use it figuratively for scattered ideas, rumors, or crowds that settle into one fixed mass, as in 'the separate accounts congealed into a single story.'
